title: What Is It Worth?
briefing: Congratulations on the promotion. Your first piece of work as a Risk Analyst comes from Hollis Varga, Finance Director.

Harrowgate warehouse sits in a flood zone. A supplier has quoted for flood barriers and Operations want them. Hollis wants to know what the flood risk is worth to Valtren and whether the barriers pay for themselves. Use the Loss Scenarios and Cost-Benefit tools at your workstation if it helps.

context.text: Hollis mentions the fleet indicators you designed: "That is the kind of thing I want: numbers that change a decision."
Cash is tighter than at the start of the year after recent incidents. Hollis will look hard at any spend.

evidence.title: Insurer's flood loss scenarios for Harrowgate
body: Minor flood (water in the loading bays, some stock lost): annual probability 4%, loss 120,000.
Major flood (warehouse inundated, four weeks closed): annual probability 1%, loss 1,600,000.
The two scenarios are mutually exclusive in any one year.

evidence.title: Property insurance schedule (flood section)
body: Insurer: Brantwell Mutual. Flood excess: 250,000 per event. Flood cover limit: 1,000,000 per event.
Valtren pays the first 250,000 of any flood loss, and anything above 1,250,000.

evidence.title: Flood barrier quote
body: Demountable barriers and a sump pump: 45,000 installed, then 3,000 a year for storage, testing and maintenance.
With barriers in place the insurer's engineer estimates: minor flood loss falls to 20,000; major flood loss falls to 600,000. Probabilities are unchanged.

evidence.title: Finance policy (extract)
evidence.body: Projects are appraised over 5 years at an 8% discount rate. Spend above an analyst's approval authority goes to the Finance Director.

questions.prompt: What is Harrowgate's expected annual flood loss today, before insurance?

mistakes.feedback: That is the major flood only; the minor flood adds 4,800.
That adds the losses without weighting by probability. Expected loss is a probability-weighted average.
That is the worst case, not the expected loss. Report the two separately.

questions.prompt: What expected annual loss does Valtren keep after insurance (excess 250,000, limit 1,000,000)?
questions.explanation: Minor floods are below the excess, so Valtren keeps all 120,000 (4,800 a year). For a major flood the insurer pays 1,000,000 and Valtren keeps 600,000 (6,000 a year).

mistakes.feedback: Insurance pays most of a major flood; the loss Valtren keeps is lower.
The cover limit is 1,000,000 and the excess applies: Valtren still keeps 600,000 of a major flood.

questions.prompt: With barriers the loss Valtren keeps falls to 3,300 a year. What does the 5-year appraisal at 8% show?

options.label: NPV about -27,000 on the losses Valtren keeps: not justified on money alone
options.feedback: Benefit 7,500 a year for 5 years at 8% is worth about 29,900; cost is 45,000 plus 3,000 a year (about 57,000). NPV about -27,000.

options.label: NPV about -1,100 on gross losses: essentially break-even, so the barriers pay for themselves
options.feedback: The gross figure counts savings the insurer would make, not Valtren. Unless the premium falls, Valtren does not get that benefit.

options.label: Strongly positive: a single major flood would cost more than thirty years of the barrier's costs
options.feedback: Comparing a certain cost with a worst case ignores how unlikely that worst case is.

options.label: No reliable answer: flood timing is unknown, so discounting future savings is meaningless here
options.feedback: Expected loss exists precisely to appraise risks whose timing is unknown.

questions.prompt: What do you do? Your approval authority as a Risk Analyst is 25,000.

options.label: Approve the barriers (45,000) now: Operations want them and the site is in a flood zone
options.feedback: Above your authority, and the appraisal does not support it.

options.label: Fund a 6,000 flood response plan (raised racking, sandbags, stock-move drill) and ask Brantwell for a lower excess
options.feedback: Cheap, within your authority, and it cuts the loss you keep. The excess quote tests the other lever.

schedules.description: Heavy rain floods Harrowgate's loading bays

options.label: Escalate the barrier case to Hollis with the appraisal and how the answer changes if flood probability doubles
options.feedback: Properly escalated, and the sensitivity is useful. The appraisal itself still argues against the barriers today.

options.label: Take no action: 10,800 a year retained is well inside the site's maintenance budget
options.feedback: The average is small but a major flood would cost Valtren 600,000 in one year. Cheap mitigations were available.

schedules.description: Heavy rain floods Harrowgate's loading bays; stock is still on the floor

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs in your paper to Hollis?

options.label: "Floods cost us 10,800 a year on average after insurance, but a major flood would cost us 600,000 in one year."
options.feedback: Expected loss and worst case side by side, neither mistaken for the other.

options.label: "After insurance, Harrowgate's flood risk costs Valtren about 10,800 a year: small against the site's turnover."
options.feedback: Presenting the average alone hides the 600,000 year.

options.label: "A major flood at Harrowgate could cost 1.6 million, so we should invest in protection now."
options.feedback: Gross worst case alone overstates what Valtren keeps and says nothing about likelihood.

options.label: "Floods are a 1-in-20-year event at Harrowgate and insurance covers the major case, so no action is needed."
options.feedback: Low likelihood is not low risk when the impact is severe.

lesson: Quantify what the organisation actually keeps after insurance, appraise treatments on that, and always report the worst case next to the expected loss.
